intro.title: Environmental management at a glance
intro.body: This page shows how your organisation affects the environment and what needs doing. Start with **Needs follow-up**: each line opens the records behind it.
steps: Register the environmental aspects of your main activities and score them.
Give every significant aspect controls, and every emergency situation a plan.
Measure energy, water, waste and emissions, and compare them with your targets.

why.body: ISO 14001 asks you to know your significant aspects, control them, be prepared for emergencies, meet your legal requirements and check with data that things improve. Auditors start here: they look for a complete register, tested emergency plans, evaluated obligations and monitoring that shows progress.

intro.title: The register of aspects and impacts
intro.body: An **environmental aspect** is the part of an activity that interacts with the environment, such as fuel use or waste water. The **impact** is the change it causes, such as climate emissions or water pollution. Each aspect gets a score, so you see which ones are **significant** and must be controlled.
steps: Pick an activity and list its aspects in normal operation, abnormal operation and emergencies.
Score each aspect with the assessment method.
Link the laws that apply and the controls for the significant ones.

why.body: Clause 6.1.2 requires you to determine the aspects you can control and those you can influence, with their impacts and a life cycle perspective, and to decide which are significant using set criteria. Significant aspects drive objectives and operational controls, so the register must be kept up to date when activities change.

empty.title: No environmental aspects yet
empty.body: Start with the activities that use the most energy, water or materials, or create the most waste. Describe the activity and let the assistant suggest typical aspects that you check and adjust.

intro.title: Registering an aspect
intro.body: Describe the **activity**, the **aspect** (what interacts with the environment) and the **impact** (what changes). Then score it against your criteria. The score and significance update as you go.
steps: Describe the activity and the aspect in plain words.
Choose the type of impact, the operating condition and the life cycle stages.
Score every criterion, link the obligations that apply and describe the controls.

why.body: A fixed method makes aspects comparable, so you can explain to an auditor why one aspect is significant and another is not. Linking the obligations shows which laws apply (6.1.3), and controls next to the aspect show that significant aspects are managed (8.1).

activity.help: The activity, product or service the aspect belongs to. Be specific enough that others recognise it.
activity.example: Washing company vehicles at the depot.

process.help: The process in Processes that the activity is part of. The process page then lists the aspect.

aspect.help: The part of the activity that interacts with the environment: something that goes in or comes out.
aspect.example: Discharge of wash water with detergent and oil.

impact.help: The change in the environment the aspect causes or can cause, good or bad.
impact.example: Pollution of the nearby stream and harm to life in the water.

condition.help: Normal operation is the daily routine. Abnormal operation is start-up, shut-down or maintenance. An emergency is an accident such as a spill or a fire.
condition.example: Overfilling a tank while refilling is an emergency.

control_level.help: Whether you control the aspect directly, or can only influence it, for example through suppliers, customers or product design.
control_level.example: Emissions from your own boilers are direct; emissions when customers use the product are indirect.

lifecycle_stages.help: The stages of the life cycle where the aspect arises. You do not need a full life cycle assessment, only the stages you can control or influence.
lifecycle_stages.example: Packaging waste arises after use and in waste treatment.

scores.help: Score each criterion on your scale. Each option says what the score means. When all criteria are scored, the total is compared with the threshold.
scores.example: Severity 4, probability 3, extent 2 and concern 4 give a weighted sum of 13.

obligations.help: The laws, permits and other requirements from Laws and regulations that apply to the aspect. With the default method, an aspect with an obligation is always significant.
obligations.example: A discharge permit limits oil in the waste water.

override.help: Use this only when the method gives a result you have good reason to disagree with. Explain why, so the decision can be reviewed.
override.example: Scored low, but neighbours have complained about it.

operational_controls.help: How the aspect is kept under control: procedures, equipment, checks, training and who is responsible. Link the procedure itself from the aspect page.
operational_controls.example: Oil separator emptied every quarter; washing only on the sealed area; monthly visual check.

status.help: Draft while you are still working on the aspect; Active when it is part of the register; Retired when the activity no longer exists.
status.example: Set Retired when the old production line is closed.

review_due_at.help: When the aspect is reviewed again. Left empty, it is set to a year from now.
review_due_at.example: Review before the new production line starts.

intro.title: Keeping an aspect under control
intro.body: This page shows the aspect, its score and why it is or is not significant, the laws that apply and what controls it. Yellow boxes at the top say what is missing and have a button that fixes it.
steps: Check the score and the reasons for significance.
Make sure significant aspects have controls: link a procedure, process or objective.
Link the obligations that apply, and an emergency plan for emergency situations.

why.body: Significant aspects must be taken into account when you set objectives and plan actions, and they must be controlled in operation. The history of every change and review shows that the register is a living tool, not a one-off exercise.

intro.title: Be prepared before it happens
intro.body: An emergency plan describes a **scenario** that could harm people or the environment, such as a chemical spill, a fire or a flood, and the **response**: who does what, with which equipment, and who to alert. Drills test that the plan works.
steps: Write a plan for each emergency situation in the aspects register.
Describe the response, the resources and the emergency contacts.
Set a drill rhythm and record what you learn from each drill.

why.body: Both ISO 14001 and ISO 45001 require you to prepare for and respond to emergencies, test the planned response regularly, and review it after drills and real events. Recorded drills are the evidence auditors ask for.

empty.title: No emergency plans yet
empty.body: Look at the aspects with "Emergency" as operating condition, and start with the scenario that would do the most harm. The assistant can draft a response that you adapt.

intro.title: Writing an emergency plan
intro.body: Keep it short and practical: someone under pressure must be able to follow it. Describe the scenario, the first actions, how to limit the impact, the equipment needed and who to contact.
steps: Describe the scenario and the possible impact, and link the aspects it covers.
Write the response as numbered steps, or let the assistant draft it.
Add the contacts and set how often the plan is tested.

why.body: A plan that is linked to the aspects it covers shows that every emergency situation is prepared for. A fixed drill rhythm gives the owner a task when the next drill is due.

title.help: A short name for the emergency, so people find the plan quickly.

scenario.help: What could happen, where and how. One or two sentences.
scenario.example: A hose bursts while refilling the diesel tank and diesel runs towards the drain.

potential_impact.help: The harm to people and the environment if nothing is done.
potential_impact.example: Diesel in the stream; fire risk; fumes for the staff.

aspects.help: The aspects in the register whose abnormal or emergency situations the plan handles. Those aspects then no longer show "No emergency plan".

response_procedure.help: What to do, in order. Short, numbered steps that work under stress.
response_procedure.example: 1. Stop the pump. 2. Close the drain cover. 3. Use the spill kit. 4. Call the site manager.

resources.help: The equipment and people needed, and where the equipment is kept.
resources.example: Spill kit at the fuel pump; drain cover in the workshop.

contacts.help: Who to call: people in the organisation, emergency services, authorities and specialist contractors.
contacts.example: Site manager, the fire service, the municipality.

status.help: Draft while you are still writing the plan; Active when it is in use (only active plans count as covering an aspect); Retired when it is no longer needed.
status.example: Active once the plan has been shown to the people involved.

drill_rrule.help: How often the plan is tested. The owner gets a task when the next drill is due.
drill_rrule.example: Once a year, plus a tabletop exercise every spring.

intro.title: Testing and improving the plan
intro.body: Record every drill, tabletop exercise and **real event**. If something did not work, tick "The plan must be revised": the owner then gets a task. Findings can become a deviation or a task with one click.
steps: Record drills and events with their outcome and who took part.
Create a deviation or a task from the findings.
Mark the plan as reviewed when it has been updated.

why.body: Clause 8.2 asks you to test the response periodically and review it after drills and emergencies. Drills with participants, findings and follow-up are the evidence that the plan works.

kind.help: A drill is a practical exercise; a tabletop exercise is a walk-through around a table; a real event is something that actually happened.
kind.example: A spill during refilling is a real event.

outcome.help: How well the response worked, honestly. "Worked partly" is useful: it shows what to improve.
outcome.example: Worked partly: the spill kit was not where the plan said.

participants.help: The people in the organisation who took part. Add others (contractors, visitors) as a number.
participants.example: The workshop team and the site manager.

findings.help: What you observed: what worked and what did not.
findings.example: It took eight minutes to find the drain cover.

intro.title: Measure what matters
intro.body: An **indicator** is something you measure regularly, such as electricity in kWh or waste in kg. With a **target** you see at once whether the trend goes the right way.
steps: Create indicators for the significant aspects: energy, fuel, water, waste.
Set a target and a baseline for each one.
Record values regularly and attach the invoice or meter reading.

why.body: Clause 9.1.1 requires you to decide what to monitor and measure, how, and against which criteria, and to keep documented evidence. Targets, baselines and attached invoices make the numbers trustworthy.

empty.title: No indicators yet
empty.body: Start with electricity and fuel: the invoices already contain the numbers. Then add water and waste.

intro.title: Setting up an indicator
intro.body: Say what is measured, in which unit and how. Set a **target** and a **baseline** so the numbers can be judged. If the indicator causes greenhouse gas emissions, add the emission category and an emission factor with its source.
steps: Name the indicator and choose the unit.
Set the target, the target year and a baseline year.
Add the emission category (scope) and the emission factor with its source.

why.body: Monitoring must be judged against criteria (9.1.1). A target with a year and a baseline turns a list of numbers into evidence of improvement, and a documented factor source makes the emission figures traceable.

name.help: What is measured, in words anyone understands.

unit.help: The unit you record values in. Use the unit on the invoice or meter.

measurement_method.help: Where the number comes from and how it is measured, so the next person does it the same way.
measurement_method.example: Monthly invoice from the grid company; main meter in the basement.

direction.help: Whether less is better (energy, waste) or more is better (share of waste sorted).

target_value.help: The yearly value you aim for, in the indicator's unit. The status compares the last 12 months with it.

baseline_value.help: The yearly value you start from, and the year it was measured. It shows how far you have come.

ghg_scope.help: Scope 1 is direct emissions from your own sources, scope 2 is purchased energy, and scope 3 is the rest of the value chain.
ghg_scope.example: Diesel for your own vans is scope 1; electricity is scope 2.

emission_factor.help: Kilograms of CO₂ equivalents per unit. Each measurement keeps the factor it was recorded with.
emission_factor.example: 2.68 kg CO₂e per litre of diesel.

factor_source.help: Where the factor comes from, so the figure can be checked.

collection_rrule.help: How often the owner is reminded to record a value.

intro.title: Following an indicator
intro.body: The top card shows the target against the last 12 months. The chart shows the trend with the target as a dashed line. Record new values with **Record value**, and attach the invoice or meter photo as evidence.
steps: Record values for each period, with their source.
Attach the evidence to each measurement.
Link the indicator to an environmental objective or a KPI.

why.body: Measurements with a source and an attached invoice are documented evidence of monitoring (9.1.1). Linking the indicator to an objective shows how you follow up your environmental objectives.

period.help: The period the value covers, from one day to one year. Use the period on the invoice.
period.example: 1–31 October for a monthly electricity invoice.

source.help: Where the value comes from. An invoice or a meter reading is better evidence than an estimate.

intro.title: Your greenhouse gas emissions
intro.body: Emissions are calculated from the indicators that have an emission factor and an emission category (scope). A category without data says **Not mapped**, which is not the same as zero.
steps: Check that the indicators that cause emissions have a factor and a category.
Compare with last year.
Download the CSV for reports.

why.body: Following the emissions year by year shows whether the organisation reduces its climate impact, and supports objectives for energy and climate. The list of indicators left out shows where the picture is incomplete.

empty.title: No emissions yet
empty.body: Add an emission factor and an emission category to the indicators that cause emissions, and record values.

intro.title: Your assessment method
intro.body: The method decides when an aspect is **significant**. Describe each criterion and what each score means: assessors see the descriptions, so different people score the same way.
steps: Choose the scale and the threshold.
Describe each criterion and each score.
Save: every aspect is scored again, and the change log shows it.

why.body: Clause 6.1.2 requires set criteria for significance. Documented criteria with described scores make the assessment consistent and easy to explain to an auditor.

method.help: Weighted sum adds the scores (with weights); product multiplies them, so one high score weighs more.

threshold.help: The score from which an aspect counts as significant.
threshold.example: 12 on a scale where the maximum is 20.

weight.help: How much the criterion counts in a weighted sum. 1 is normal; 2 counts double.

criteria.help: What you judge each aspect on, such as severity, probability, extent and the concern of interested parties.
criteria.example: Severity: how much harm the impact can do.

aspects-and-impacts.title: Aspects and impacts in plain words

sections.heading: Cause and effect
sections.body: An **aspect** is the cause: the part of an activity that interacts with the environment, such as burning fuel, using water or creating waste. The **impact** is the effect: climate change, water shortage, pollution. One aspect can have several impacts.

sections.heading: Normal, abnormal and emergency
sections.body: Look at each activity in **normal** operation, in **abnormal** conditions such as start-up, shut-down and maintenance, and in an **emergency** such as a spill or a fire. Emergencies often have the largest impact and need an emergency plan.

sections.heading: A life cycle perspective
sections.body: Think beyond your own gate: raw materials, design, production, transport, use, what happens after use and waste treatment. You do not need a full life cycle assessment, but consider the stages you **control** and those you can **influence**, for example through suppliers or product design.

quiz.question: Which of these is an environmental aspect, not an impact?
quiz.explanation: The exhaust is the part of the activity that interacts with the environment. Air pollution and climate change are the impacts it causes.

quiz.question: A chemical tank can overflow while it is being filled. Which operating condition is this?
quiz.explanation: An overflow is an accident, so it is an emergency that an emergency plan should cover.

sections.heading: Why significance matters
sections.body: You cannot control everything equally. **Significant** aspects are the ones you must take into account when you set objectives, plan actions and design operational controls.

sections.heading: Scores against criteria
sections.body: Each aspect is scored against your criteria, such as severity, probability, extent and the concern of interested parties. Each score has a description, so everyone scores the same way. The scores are combined and compared with a **threshold**. A law that applies can make an aspect significant on its own.

sections.heading: When you disagree with the result
sections.body: Sometimes the method gives a result that does not fit, for example when neighbours complain about noise that scores low. You can set the significance by hand, but you must give a reason, and the original result stays visible.

quiz.question: The method says an aspect is not significant, but the authorities have asked you to reduce it. What should you do?
options: Mark it as significant by hand and explain why
quiz.explanation: Setting it by hand with a reason corrects the result and documents why.

sections.heading: Plan the response
sections.body: For each possible emergency, describe what to do first, how to limit the harm to people and the environment, which equipment is needed and who to alert. Link the plan to the aspects it covers. Keep it short enough to use under stress.

sections.heading: Test it
sections.body: A plan that has never been tested is a guess. Hold **drills** or **tabletop exercises** on a fixed rhythm, and treat real events as tests too. Each drill is recorded with its outcome, participants, findings and lessons learned.

sections.heading: Learn and revise
sections.body: When a drill shows that something does not work, such as a missing spill kit or an unclear role, tick "The plan must be revised" and create a deviation or task from the findings. Both ISO 14001 and ISO 45001 require the plan to be reviewed after drills and events.

quiz.question: A drill showed that nobody knew where the spill kit was. What is the best next step?
options: Record the drill as worked well
Record it as worked partly, and revise the plan and the training
quiz.explanation: The drill revealed a weakness. Recording it honestly and revising the plan is exactly what drills are for.

sections.heading: Choose what to measure
sections.body: Measure what is linked to the significant aspects and the objectives: energy, fuel, water, waste and materials. Decide the unit, where the data comes from, how often values are recorded, and the **target** you compare them with.

sections.heading: From values to CO₂e
sections.body: An **emission factor** converts a value into kilograms of CO₂ equivalents, for example litres of diesel into kg CO₂e. Write down where the factor comes from. Each measurement keeps the factor it was recorded with, so an updated factor does not change earlier years.

sections.heading: Scope 1, 2 and 3
sections.body: **Scope 1** is direct emissions from your own sources, **scope 2** is purchased electricity and heat, and **scope 3** is everything else in the value chain, such as travel and transport. Start with scope 1 and 2, where the data is easiest to get. A scope with no data is "not mapped", not zero.

quiz.question: Which scope do emissions from purchased electricity belong to?
quiz.explanation: Purchased electricity, heating and cooling are scope 2: indirect emissions from energy you buy.

quiz.question: You update the emission factor for electricity. What happens to last year's emissions?
options: They are recalculated with the new factor
They keep the factor that applied at the time
quiz.explanation: Each measurement keeps the factor it was recorded with, so historical figures stay the same.

aspects.title: Register an aspect
aspects.body: Start here. Describe an activity and let the assistant suggest its usual aspects.

aspects.title: Focus on what matters
aspects.body: Filter on status, significance or what needs follow-up. More filters and grouping by activity are under "More filters".

plans.title: Plan for emergencies
plans.body: Create a plan for each serious scenario. The assistant can draft the response.

plans.title: Find the right plans
plans.body: Filter on status, or show the plans whose drill or review is overdue.

metrics.title: Create an indicator
metrics.body: Say what is measured, the unit, the target and the emission factor.

metrics.title: Filter the indicators
metrics.body: Show one category, the indicators that are off target, or one emission category.

environmental-aspect.definition: An element of an organisation's activities, products or services that interacts or can interact with the environment.

significant-aspect.definition: An aspect that has or can have a significant environmental impact, decided with the organisation's own criteria.

compliance-obligation.definition: A law, permit or other requirement the organisation must or has chosen to comply with.

operational-control.definition: What keeps an aspect under control in daily work: procedures, equipment, checks and training.

emergency-preparedness.definition: Being ready to respond to accidents and emergencies, with a tested plan, equipment and trained people.

emission-factor.definition: The greenhouse gas emissions caused by one unit of an activity, in kilograms of CO₂ equivalents per unit.

ghg-scope.definition: Scope 1: direct emissions from your own sources. Scope 2: purchased energy. Scope 3: the rest of the value chain.
